profiles.title: Blanco tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Blanco tequila born in the town of Tequila and the valley that carries its name, from 100% blue agave grown in the same ground. The valley sits lower than Los Altos and its nights are warmer, so its agave tends to grow smaller and more herbaceous, and a valley blanco usually tastes more savoury and green than sweet. The valley is proud of that difference.
profiles.description: Expect roasted piña first, then citrus, black pepper and fresh green notes. A blanco (also called silver or plata) is typically bottled without oak aging; the rules allow brief rests below the reposado minimum, but the style lives on the distilled agave itself, with nothing in the way.
profiles.finish: Clean and peppery, with citrus and a gentle vegetal warmth that fades steadily.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (oven/autoclave), tahona or roller-mill extraction, fermented in open tanks, double distilled; typically unaged, though blanco rules permit brief oak contact below the two-month reposado minimum
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is a legal class of tequila typically sold unaged, though the rules permit brief oak maturation below the reposado minimum
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? Start here: no barrel stands between you and the cooked agave, so a blanco is the clearest way to taste each producer's land in the glass.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass or with a lime wheel; also the classic Margarita and Paloma base. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the savoury roasted-agave centre and the clean, peppery finish.

profiles.whyItTastes: That savoury, earthy edge comes from place and method together. Valley agave tends to grow smaller and more herbaceous than highland agave, and traditional valley producers crush the cooked piña with a tahona stone wheel and ferment in open tanks. Age and price have nothing to do with it.

profiles.title: Espadín mezcal, Valles Centrales style
profiles.context: Joven mezcal from espadín (Agave angustifolia) in the Valles Centrales around Oaxaca, made the artisanal way. Here mezcal is family work: agave hearts roasted in earthen pit ovens, small batches, and a craft each palenque hands to the next generation. Espadín is the most widely planted mezcal agave, the one a Oaxacan family is likely to pour first for a curious visitor, because it's the friendliest way into the tradition. The smoke of the pit roast is part of what home tastes like here, and Oaxacans are proud of it.
profiles.description: Expect roasted agave and smoke first, then fruit, herbs and a mineral-like edge that change with the village, the maestro mezcalero and the batch. Mezcal can be made from many agave species, not only blue agave, and not every mezcal is pit-roasted or smoky; this style is, because the piñas cook underground. Bottles from the same valley still vary widely.
profiles.smoke: Gentle to moderate smoke from the pit-roast, woven through the fruit and herb notes rather than dominating them.
profiles.finish: Long and dry, with smoke that lingers softly and fades into earthy herbs.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (espadín, cultivated)
profiles.process: Earthen-pit roast, tahona or horse-drawn mill, wild-yeast fermentation, double distilled, joven (unaged)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; joven (or blanco) is its unaged legal class under NOM-070. Abocado con is a separate class, for mezcal with ingredients added
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal? The smoke comes from roasting the agave underground. It's part of the process, not an added flavour, and Oaxacans will happily tell you it tastes of home.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat at room temperature; smoke opens up in a wide glass. Editor's suggestion only.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the roast smoke as a thread through the agave, not a wall in front of it.

profiles.whyItTastes: The earthen pit cooks espadín slowly over wood, and that's where the roast and smoke come from; how much smoke depends on the wood, the time and the pit. Tahona milling and wild-yeast fermentation are part of the method too, and joven means no oak stands between you and the cook.

profiles.title: Bacanora, Agave Pacifica style (Sierra de Sonora)
profiles.context: Bacanora is Sonora's own wild agave spirit, distilled from Agave angustifolia pacifica (locally Pacifica, or Yaquiana) in the Sierra Madre de Sonora, under a denomination of origin that covers 35 Sonoran municipalities. For most of the 20th century (1915–1992, according to Sonora's official history) making it was prohibited, and families kept distilling quietly in the sierra. Production was legalized again in 1992, and the denomination of origin followed in 2000: two separate milestones. Bacanora survived because vinateros kept their vinatas going and taught the next generation, and Sonorans tell that story with pride.
profiles.description: Expect roasted agave at the centre, a gentler smoke than most Oaxacan mezcal, desert herbs and a dry, mineral-like edge. Traditional bacanora roasts the agave hearts in earthen pits, often over mesquite, ferments with wild yeasts and is distilled twice, so in the glass it often sits between tequila and Oaxacan mezcal.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia pacifica (wild-harvested; locally Pacifica or Yaquiana)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted (often mesquite-fueled), wild-yeast fermentation, double distillation
profiles.category: Bacanora — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Sonora, since 2000)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to bacanora? Think of it as mezcal's Sonoran cousin: the same roasted-agave heart, usually a little less smoke, often leaner and more herbal.
profiles.smoke: Present but usually gentler than Oaxacan mezcal: the pit roast gives a lean, savoury smoke rather than a dominant one.
profiles.finish: Dry and herbal, with a soft smoky thread and a mineral, peppery fade.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass; a short rest opens the roast aromas. A little water or one ice cube works too if you prefer it softer. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the roast-agave aromas opening after a short rest in the glass.

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild Pacifica/Yaquiana from the Sonoran sierra, pit-roasted (often over mesquite) and wild-fermented. Producers and reviewers describe an herbal, gently smoky character and credit the plant and the pit roast together; take it as a tendency of the style, because wild harvest doesn't guarantee it. Double distillation is the standard method here, and on its own it doesn't make a spirit cleaner.

profiles.title: Sierra raicilla, Maximiliana style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is Jalisco's mountain spirit, and jaliscienses pour it as proof that their state makes more than tequila. Its denomination of origin (2019) also reaches exactly one Nayarit municipality, Bahía de Banderas on the Jalisco border, not all Nayarit. There are two traditions: Sierra raicilla, made mainly from Agave maximiliana and inaequidens cooked in above-ground ovens, and Costa raicilla, from angustifolia and rhodacantha cooked in underground pits. For decades raicilla was made informally in the shadow of its famous neighbour, and the people of the sierra kept it alive until the law caught up. This is the Sierra style of the Sierra Occidental.
profiles.description: Expect orchard fruit, herbs and a soft lactic roundness with a gently funky, fermented edge, and less smoke than pit-roasted spirits. Sierra raicilla is usually cooked in above-ground adobe ovens rather than pits, fermented with wild yeasts in wooden vats and distilled in small rustic tabernas (the word names the distillery, not the still). Each maestro's batches vary widely.
profiles.plant: Agave maximiliana (wild-harvested; Sierra raicilla's signature agave)
profiles.process: Above-ground adobe-oven roast, open wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to raicilla? Expect an agave spirit that's often funkier and fruitier than tequila and usually lighter on smoke than mezcal, Sierra raicilla especially. It's Jalisco's other pride.
profiles.smoke: Usually light in the Sierra style: above-ground ovens give a faint roast note rather than pit smoke.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, gently funky, with orchard fruit and a soft sweet-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; its gentle funk also works in a Negroni-style serve (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the gentle fermented edge that makes sierra raicilla its own thing.

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild maximiliana from Jalisco's mountains, roasted in above-ground adobe ovens instead of pits, which is why there's less smoke than in the pit traditions. Then come open fermentation in wooden vats and small-batch distillation. Plant, oven and batch size together give the rustic, herbal edge; no single step explains it.

profiles.title: Tuxca, Liñeno/Cimarrón style (Jalisco–Colima borderlands)
profiles.context: Tuxca belongs to the borderlands of southern Jalisco and northern Colima, below the Volcán de Colima, and takes its name from the municipality of Tuxcacuesco. It has no denomination of origin, and the communities that keep it (Tuxcacuesco, the Río Almería valley, Zapotitlán de Vadillo, Tolimán) are content for the name to stay regional rather than legal. They make it the old way, and quietly. Colima's part in this story is the borderland itself: the tradition, the volcano's slopes and the Río Almería valley cross the state line. The cited example bottle is made in Jalisco, and this guide makes no claim of Colima production coverage beyond what its sources document.
profiles.description: Expect a lean, spicy, mineral-like spirit rather than a smoky-sweet one. Tuxca is defined less by a legal category than by its method: wild agaves (often Liñeño/Cimarrón, Agave angustifolia and relatives) roasted in cylindrical pits, mashed by hand, fermented in volcanic stone craters and distilled in wooden Filipino stills.
profiles.plant: Wild agaves, often Liñeno/Cimarrón (Agave angustifolia and local relatives); ensambles vary by vinatero
profiles.process: Cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation
profiles.category: Tuxca — a regional tradition with no denomination of origin; legal status is not equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tuxca? Expect a deeply traditional borderlands spirit without certification: leaner and more mineral than most mezcal, with spice instead of smoke. You won't find a DO certification seal on the bottle, though other labelling requirements still apply; the tradition's authority is cultural rather than certified.
profiles.smoke: Usually light: the pit roast is shorter and the wooden stills read herbal-spicy rather than smoky.
profiles.finish: Dry and spicy, with lime and pepper fading to volcanic mineral.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat alongside water; lean and mineral, it suits slow sipping (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the lean mineral spine and how slowly the glass opens.

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild Liñeño/Cimarrón agaves, a cylindrical pit roast, hand-mashing, fermentation in a volcanic stone crater and a wooden Filipino still. Few traditions follow such a specific chain, and the cooked, wild character it leaves changes from batch to batch with the agave mix.

profiles.title: Comiteco, aguamiel style (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco belongs to Comitán, Chiapas. Instead of cooking agave hearts, producers collect the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey comiteco, ferment it and distil it. Since 6 October 2025 the name “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas” has been protected as an Indicación Geográfica, a legal protection distinct from a denomination of origin. It covers a spirit made from maguey comiteco (identified as Agave americana L. in the declaration; some references also name Agave atrovirens) together with cane sugars in the Meseta Comiteca-Tojolabal. Cane sugar is part of the protected definition, and an honest bottle tells you what's in it.
profiles.description: Expect green, lactic, gently herbal notes from the fermented sap, and none of the roast or smoke of pit-roasted spirits, because the agave is never cooked. In character it sits closer to a distilled pulque than to mezcal, though it's a tradition of its own. Recipes vary between producers and are disclosed bottle by bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey comiteco (Agave americana L. per the 2025 IG declaration; some references name Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled — no cooking of the piña
profiles.category: Comiteco — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas, protected since October 2025 as the Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas”; an IG is a different legal figure from tequila's or mezcal's denomination of origin
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco? Forget smoke: this is a sap spirit, green, lactic and herbal, from uncooked agave. It's Comitán's own tradition, and unlike the cooked-agave spirits most people meet first.
profiles.finish: Smooth and herbal, with a light earthy fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Neat at room temperature, in a small glass; its green, lactic character also suits a meal shared slowly. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the green, lactic sap character — nothing here was roasted.

profiles.whyItTastes: No roast at all: the sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey comiteco is collected, fermented and distilled, alongside the cane sugar the definition allows. That sap path is why comiteco tastes nothing like a cooked-heart spirit.

profiles.title: Destilado de pulque, Salmiana style (Tlaxcala)
profiles.context: Tlaxcala holds pulque close: it's the heartland of the maguey pulquero. Destilado de pulque is the region's distilled sap spirit. Producers ferment the aguamiel of the maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana) into pulque and then distil it, and the agave is never cooked. Tlaxcala isn't part of the mezcal denomination and destilado de pulque isn't a certified category; it's a regional tradition sold under destilado labels, kept by families for whom distilling pulque is part of the heritage of their hills. Pulque itself, undistilled, isn't part of this spirit catalogue.
profiles.description: Expect fresh, green, lactic and faintly wild notes, with pulque's vegetal tang carried into the glass instead of roast or smoke. Tasters report a wide, unusual range, from steamed grass and sour-candy acidity to creamed-corn sweetness. That signature comes from distilling a fermented sap rather than a cooked agave mash.
profiles.plant: Maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana); sap collected daily from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel fermented into pulque (about 48 hours), then distilled; the piña is never cooked
profiles.category: Destilado de pulque — a regional tradition; no denomination of origin, and explicitly not mezcal (fermented pulque is not a distilled spirit)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to destilado de pulque? It's distilled pulque: uncooked agave sap, so expect lactic, green, gently sour notes unlike any cooked-agave spirit. A taste of Tlaxcala's pulque country.
profiles.finish: Light and tangy, with lactic and green notes that fade quickly.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, chilled slightly; its lactic tang suits an open mind (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the fresh pulque kinship — lactic, yeasty, unlike any cooked agave.

profiles.whyItTastes: Aguamiel from the living maguey pulquero ferments into pulque (about 48 hours) and is then distilled; the piña is never cooked. The flavour follows the sap, not a roast.

profiles.title: Costa raicilla, coastal style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: On the Jalisco coast, around Cabo Corrientes and Tomatlán, raicilla is made mainly from Agave angustifolia (locally chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha, and coastal tabernas cook it the old way, in underground pits. Raicilla's denomination of origin (2019) covers 16 Jalisco municipalities and exactly one in Nayarit, Bahía de Banderas on the Jalisco border, rather than all Nayarit. The tradition splits into Sierra and Costa, and the coast is proud of the lean, saline character of its raicilla beside the mountain style.
profiles.description: Expect more smoke and a more savoury edge than in Sierra raicilla, with citrus and herbs alongside the pit roast. The difference is in the cook: coastal producers traditionally roast in underground pits, where the Sierra uses above-ground adobe ovens. Bottles vary widely, and tasting notes for the example bottle are not yet documented.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha (wild and cultivated)
profiles.process: Underground pit roast, wild-yeast fermentation, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019); Costa is an editorial tradition split, not a legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to coastal raicilla? Think of it as the smokier, pit-roasted cousin of Sierra raicilla: same DO, different cook, and the coast's own take.
profiles.smoke: More present than in Sierra raicilla: the underground pit cook gives a savoury smoke woven through citrus and herbs.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, smoky and savoury with a citrus fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; the smoke suits slow evening sipping (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the coastal herbs and smoke, lighter on the roast than valley mezcal.

profiles.whyItTastes: Coastal chico aguiar and rhodacantha, an underground pit roast and wild fermentation in the canyons of Cabo Corrientes: a different plant mix and a different roast from the Sierra tradition, which is why Costa and Sierra raicilla taste apart.

profiles.title: Reposado tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: This is the valley blanco after a rest in oak, made the traditional way. Reposado ('rested') is a legal class: at least two months in oak, with no maximum, and most producers rest it between two months and a year. Valley tradition says the rest should season the agave, never bury it, and producers here take pride in that restraint.
profiles.description: Here tequila first meets wood. The green, peppery blanco character picks up vanilla, caramel and baking spice from the barrel, while the cooked agave stays at the centre: in a traditional reposado the oak is the seasoning, not the dish, and reviewers of the example bottle find the agave still forward. Age is no ladder: a two-month reposado can taste leaner than another producer's blanco, and more oak is not better.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then rested in oak barrels (legal minimum 2 months; typically 2–12 months)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; reposado is a legal class (oak-rested, 2-month minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to reposado? Think of it as the blanco after a short rest in oak: the agave stays, and vanilla and spice join it.
profiles.finish: Medium, with gentle wood spice and a caramel-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass, or over one ice cube; its rounder base also carries a Margarita or Paloma well when you want the oak along. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: how the gentle oak sits under the agave without covering it.

profiles.whyItTastes: The same valley base as the blanco, rested in oak for at least the legal two months (usually 2–12). The oak softens the green edge and adds gentle spice without covering the cooked agave underneath.

profiles.title: Añejo tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Give the valley's tequila a year or more in oak and you have añejo ('aged'), a legal class: at least one year in barrels of no more than 600 litres, with extra añejo (three years or more) beyond it. This one is a traditionally made valley añejo of around 18 months; the NOM sets only the minimum, not a range. Valley practice favours restraint: the agave should still speak through a year of oak, and the best producers make sure it does.
profiles.description: A year or more of oak makes tequila darker, rounder and sweeter-tasting: the barrel brings vanilla, dried fruit and something close to cocoa, while the blanco's fresh green edge fades. A well-made añejo keeps cooked agave in the picture, and the example bottle's reviewers find exactly that balance. 'Older is better' is marketing, not a rule: wood depends on barrel type, size, age and climate, and plenty of drinkers prefer blanco or reposado.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then aged in oak at least one year (typically ex-bourbon casks)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 1-year minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to añejo? Expect tequila at its roundest and darkest: oak, vanilla and dried fruit around the agave. It's the closest to whiskey in feel and still tequila at heart.
profiles.finish: Long and rounded, with oak spice, sweet agave and a gentle dry fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, ideally in a small glass to concentrate the aroma (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the oak sweetness wrapping the cooked agave, and the long, soft finish.

profiles.whyItTastes: A year or more in oak, typically ex-bourbon casks. Now the wood speaks clearly, vanilla and caramel over the agave.

profiles.title: Cristalino tequila style
profiles.context: Cristalino looks like a blanco but starts as an aged tequila, usually reposado or añejo, filtered (typically through charcoal) to remove the colour the barrel gave it. It isn't a legal class. Nearly every big brand now makes one, and bartenders and writers argue over whether it's innovation or a marketing-driven dilution of tradition. That argument is part of how Mexico debates, with pride, what its spirits should be.
profiles.description: In the glass it's as clear as a blanco, but it tastes of softened barrel: rounder, creamier and often sweeter than either a blanco or its unfiltered aged base, with gentler acidity and less agave bite. Filtration removes colour and, with it, some flavour, and what's left is smooth and easy by design. Critics flag that the category is prone to additives that put back sweetness and body, so the base spirit and the producer matter more than the name.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Made as oak-rested reposado or añejo, then charcoal-filtered clear; a finishing choice, not a legal class
profiles.category: Cristalino — a finishing/marketing style on top of a legal class, not a legal class itself; disclosure of the aged base varies by brand
profiles.beginnerNote: New to cristalino? It's an aged tequila with the colour filtered out: clear like a blanco, rounder like an añejo, and much argued about.
profiles.finish: Smooth and short-to-medium; engineered for easy sipping.

placeCoords.precision: region (Jalisco, highlands/valley varies by producer); approximate

pairing.serving: Served neat or over ice; often positioned as an entry to aged tequila (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: whether the filtered oak reads smooth or thin to you — opinions genuinely differ.

profiles.whyItTastes: It's made as an oak-rested reposado or añejo and then charcoal-filtered clear. Producers say the aged character survives the filter; reviewers often find some of it goes with the colour. What's left tastes of wood but looks like a blanco.

maturation.duration: aged base (varies; typically añejo or extra añejo) then filtered

profiles.title: Comiteco añejo, glass-rested with oak branches (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: This is the aged side of comiteco, Comitán's sap spirit: the fresh aguamiel of the living maguey comiteco, fermented and distilled without cooking the plant. The example producer rests its añejo in glass with branches of white oak rather than in barrels, so the wood character comes from oak contact in glass, not barrel maturation. Añejo here is the producer's own expression. The Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas” (protected 6 October 2025) sets the rules, so check them rather than assuming aged classes don't exist.
profiles.description: Expect the same green, lactic, herbal sap character as young comiteco, with gentle oak spice and a little colour, and none of the vanilla-heavy roundness of barrel-aged spirits. Resting on white-oak branches in glass keeps the wood soft. Beside the unaged comiteco profile it tastes slightly rounder and warmer, still a long way from whiskey.
profiles.plant: Maguey comiteco (Agave americana L. per the 2025 IG declaration; some references name Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled in copper, then rested in glass with branches of white oak (no barrel maturation, no cooking of the piña)
profiles.category: Comiteco añejo — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas, protected since October 2025 as the Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas”; añejo here is a producer expression, not a legal class as it is in tequila
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco añejo? Don't expect a tequila añejo. The wood comes from oak branches resting in glass, so it's gentler: warm spice over the same green, lactic sap character.
profiles.finish: Medium-length and herbal, with a soft oak-spice fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat to let the gentle oak spice carry the herbal sap character (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the oak spice over the herbal sap, from glass-resting rather than barrels.

profiles.whyItTastes: Sap-derived like the young comiteco, then rested in glass with branches of white oak: a gentle touch of wood without barrel maturation. Añejo here is a producer expression, not a legal class like tequila's.

profiles.title: Raicilla reposado, barrel-rested style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla has a denomination of origin, and aged expressions exist (the example bottle rests in wood). The exact requirements for aged classes come from the 2019 DO declaration and the published draft standard, not from tequila's rules. This is the young-rested end: a few months in wood that round the spirit without pushing the agave aside. Jalisco's raicilleros are proud that their spirit won legal recognition without losing its rustic character, and short rests are one way they keep it.
profiles.description: Expect the fruity, floral, lightly smoky raicilla character with a light halo of vanilla, caramel and soft fruit sweetness around the agave, not in place of it. The example bottle lists a 3-month rest, and its reviewers describe sherry-cask influence with plum, raisin and sweet tobacco; they also warn that the cask can overpower the agave. That risk of wood masking the spirit is part of an honest picture of the style.
profiles.plant: Varies by bottling (the example bottle lists Angustifolia and Maximiliana); linked to the Maximiliana plant page as the Sierra tradition's signature agave — check the bottle, batches differ
profiles.process: Fermented and distilled (the example bottle lists steel), then rested in wooden barrels about 3 months
profiles.category: Raicilla reposado — an aged-class claim under the raicilla denomination of origin (2019); the aged-class rules rest on the DO declaration and the published standard project, so verify the effective version rather than assuming tequila-style minimums
profiles.beginnerNote: New to aged raicilla? Expect the fruit and flowers of a joven with a light caramel-vanilla halo from a short rest, closer to its unaged self than to tequila reposado.
profiles.smoke: A delicate smokiness can persist from production; the example bottle's reviewer notes campfire smoke on the finish.
profiles.finish: Medium to long, with sweet fruit, cinnamon-adjacent spice and a soft smoke fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; a short-rested raicilla also works where a fruity reposado is called for (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: how the fruit carries through the rest.

profiles.whyItTastes: Fermented and distilled (the example bottle lists steel), then rested in wooden barrels for about three months. That's this bottle's choice, not a legal minimum, and the short rest rounds the raicilla without turning it into something else.

profiles.title: Extra añejo tequila, highland style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Extra añejo ('extra aged') is tequila's newest legal class: at least three years in oak barrels of no more than 600 litres, added to the NOM in 2006. Producers pushed for it because they were already resting tequila that long; El Tesoro's family released its Paradiso in 1994, before the class existed. This one is a highland extra añejo of four to five years, well past the three-year minimum (the NOM sets a minimum, not a range). Growers in Los Altos describe their agave as bigger and sweeter, and some alteños say it carries long rests better than valley agave. That's a local view, and valley distilleries make extra añejo too.
profiles.description: Three or more years of oak take tequila towards brandy: deep oak, chocolate, coffee and dried fruit around a cooked-agave core. The tension in this class is that many producers think anything past about four years is too much, because wood can drown the agave. The best keep agave in the picture, as the example bottle's reviewers find. 'Older is better' is still marketing, not a rule.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated; highland mineral soils)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (or stone-roasted by some traditionalists), fermented, double distilled, then aged at least three years in oak (typically American ex-bourbon barrels)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; extra añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 3-year minimum, barrels up to 600 litres)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to extra añejo? This is tequila at its most whiskey-like: expect oak, chocolate and coffee. The good ones still taste of agave underneath.
profiles.finish: Long and oaky, with chocolate, gentle spice and a slow agave fade.

placeCoords.precision: municipality (Arandas, Los Altos; example producer La Alteña); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat after dinner, in a snifter-style glass (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: how much agave survives the long rest — the best ones keep it in the frame.

profiles.whyItTastes: Highland agave from red mineral soils tends to be sweeter and more floral than valley agave, though place doesn't guarantee it. Three or more years in oak, typically American ex-bourbon, pull the spirit firmly into wood, with the highland fruit holding on underneath.

profiles.title: Mezcal reposado, briefly barrel-rested espadín style (Valles Centrales, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Reposado is one of the six mezcal classes in NOM-070-SCFI-2016 (blanco o joven, madurado en vidrio, reposado, añejo, abocado con and destilado con): a rest of two months to a year in wood. Most mezcal sold around the world is joven, and many Oaxacan traditionalists argue that wood hides what makes mezcal distinct; they defend the pit roast because it tastes of their land. Aged mezcal is still a growing, legal part of the category. This is the short-rested end: a few months in wood, usually starting from pit-roasted espadín.
profiles.description: Expect espadín's pit-roast smoke, softened, with light vanilla and caramel over it and the vegetal, roasted character still there. Reviewers of the example bottle describe exactly that balance, smoke from nose to finish ending in a smoky butterscotch, while others caution that the wood can dominate. Mezcal first, wood second: if the wood leads, it's drifting towards tequila reposado.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (espadín, cultivated); some producers blend wild agaves
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled, then rested in oak 2-12 months (the example bottle lists 4-6 months in American oak)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own denomination of origin; reposado is a legal class (wood-rested, 2–12 months; the wood need not be oak, and the two-month start coincides with tequila's although the other requirements differ)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal reposado? Expect the smoke of a joven softened with vanilla and caramel: a gentler way into smoky agave spirits.
profiles.smoke: The pit-roast smoke of espadín mezcal persists through the rest; reviewers describe it from nose to finish.
profiles.finish: Medium, smoky-sweet, with a butterscotch-adjacent fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Tlacolula valley, Valles Centrales, Oaxaca); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; also works in margaritas where a smoky reposado is welcome (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: how the wood rounds the smoke without erasing it.

profiles.whyItTastes: The same pit-roasted espadín base as the joven, rested in oak for 2–12 months (the example bottle lists 4–6 in American oak): the roast stays, softened by wood. Tequila and mezcal reposado both start at two months, but their other requirements differ, so don't carry rules from one spirit to the other.

profiles.title: Tobalá mezcal, wild Agave potatorum style (Sierra, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Tobalá (Agave potatorum) is a small, mostly wild agave of the high country, often called the 'king of agaves' in México. It's tiny and slow to mature (a variable, source-dependent range often cited around 12–15 years), so yields are very low, which has pushed prices up and wild populations down. The mezcal DO permits any agave species, so tobalá is mezcal; some tobalá is now cultivated, which changes both the sustainability story and, reviewers note, sometimes the flavour. This style follows the plant rather than a place: tobalá grows across Oaxaca's Sierra Norte and beyond, and in the Sierra Norte finding one ready to harvest is a point of personal pride.
profiles.description: Expect a lighter, more floral mezcal than espadín: sweet citrus, tropical fruit and a silky texture over a gentler roast. Ancestral producers distil it in clay pots, and artisanal producers in copper or clay, since the artisanal category allows both. Batch variation is genuinely large; a cited blind tasting of eight tobalás found no single common thread, so think of a family of expressions rather than one flavour. The example bottle, from wild-harvested tobalá around Santiago Matatlán, is herbal and delicate, with dry soil, thyme, coriander and a touch of rosemary.
profiles.plant: Agave potatorum (tobalá; mostly wild-harvested, some cultivated — check the bottle)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled; NOM-070's artisanal category permits copper alembics or clay pots, so clay is not exclusive to ancestral production
profiles.category: Mezcal — tobalá is within the mezcal denomination of origin; it is a wild agave (Agave potatorum) under sustainability pressure, not a legal class or one of the NOM-070 production categories
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tobalá? Expect mezcal's gentler, more floral side: sweet citrus and tropical fruit over a soft roast. It costs more because the agave is small, slow and scarce.
profiles.smoke: A gentle roast character rather than heavy smoke; ancestral clay-pot batches can show more.
profiles.finish: Medium and silky, with fruit sweetness and a soft mineral fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Sierra Norte de Oaxaca; the wild style ranges across the Sierra, while the example bottle is produced in Santiago Matatlán); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat in a small copita — a small stemmed glass — so the florals gather; if you mix it, expect a quieter, gentler version rather than the whole character. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the floral lift and the silky texture — wild tobalá is often quieter than its reputation.

profiles.whyItTastes: Small wild tobalá matures over many years at altitude (often cited around 12–15, depending on the source), giving very low yields. Reviewers describe concentrated character in some batches, and the pit roast and frequent clay-pot distillation keep the cook gentle. Batch variation is genuine and large: a cited blind tasting found no single common thread.

profiles.title: Sotol, Chihuahua desert style
profiles.context: Sotol is the desert's own spirit, distilled from Dasylirion (desert spoon, sereque), native to the Chihuahuan desert. Dasylirion is a relative of agave in the Asparagaceae family that follows the same roasted-piña logic, and it's proudly not agave. Sotol has had a Denominación de Origen since 2002, covering only Chihuahua, Coahuila and Durango. Its 20th century included restrictive regulation and clandestine production in the northern sierra; the legal framing varied by era and place, and this guide asserts no single nationwide pre-1994 ban. The vinatas of the sierra kept the tradition going quietly, from one generation to the next, in the same households Chihuahuenses still pour from today. This is the Chihuahua desert style.
profiles.description: Expect bright, grassy, herbal freshness, sometimes close to menthol or eucalyptus, over a smoky, earthy base from the pit roast: more vegetal than most agave spirits. Place shows unusually clearly here. The cited DO sources describe sotol from forested areas tasting of menthol, mushrooms and pine, and sotol from the arid desert leaning to leather, cacao and pepper. One plant may give roughly one bottle after a variable number of years (often cited around 8–12), so batches are small and genuinely vary.
profiles.plant: Dasylirion (desert spoon; commonly wheeleri, cedrosanum or leiophyllum), wild-harvested; not an agave, though a close relative
profiles.process: Piña pit-roasted in conical ovens (or steam-cooked by larger producers), wild-fermented, distilled in copper or clay; whether roots are left intact depends on harvest practice, and regrowth is not guaranteed
profiles.category: Sotol — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango, since 2002); explicitly not an agave spirit, included here as an agave-adjacent northern tradition
profiles.beginnerNote: New to sotol? Expect bright wet-grass and herbal freshness over gentle smoke, closer to a green, wild cousin of mezcal than to tequila.
profiles.smoke: A gentle, usually lighter smoke than mezcal from the pit roast; batch and producer dependent.
profiles.finish: Medium, herbal and slightly tingly, with a mineral fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat in a small glass; also good with mineral sparkling water (editorial suggestion).
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the desert-herb freshness that Dasylirion gives instead of agave sweetness.

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild-harvested Dasylirion (not an agave), roasted in conical pits and fermented with wild yeasts: the earthy, smoky, herbal character follows from the plant and the desert cook together. Wild stands face documented harvest pressure; claims that they regrow need species and method evidence this guide hasn't verified.

profiles.title: Highland blanco tequila, Los Altos style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Up in Los Altos, around Atotonilco el Alto and Arandas, blanco tastes different. Red, iron-rich soils, higher ground and cooler nights tend to grow bigger, sweeter agave, so a highland blanco often leans bright, fruity and floral where the valley leans earthy and savoury. Both are simply tequila blanco, the unaged legal class; the difference is cultural and agronomic, and Los Altos is visibly proud of its red-earth fruit.
profiles.description: Sweeter cooked agave with citrus (orange peel, grapefruit), tropical and stone fruit, delicate flowers and a gentle spice, in a softer, rounder body than the valley style.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated; highland red mineral soils)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (or stone-roasted by some traditionalists), fermented, double distilled; typically unaged, though blanco rules permit brief oak contact below the two-month reposado minimum
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is a legal class of tequila typically sold unaged, though the rules permit brief oak maturation below the reposado minimum
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? A highland blanco is often a friendly place to start: soft, sweet and fruity, and usually less savoury than a valley blanco, though the two overlap and bottles vary. Try it beside the valley blanco to taste what place can do with the same plant.
profiles.finish: Soft and fruity, with a slow sweet-agave fade and a light peppery lift at the end.

placeCoords.precision: town (Atotonilco el Alto area, Los Altos); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass, or in a Margarita/Paloma where its fruit plays well with citrus. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the sweeter, floral highland fruit against the pepper.

profiles.whyItTastes: Growers in Los Altos say the altitude, the red iron-rich soils and the cooler nights give bigger, sweeter piñas, and the unaged spirit leans fruity, floral and bright rather than earthy. One blind tasting panel found that regional pattern weaker than folklore suggests, so take it as a tendency.

profiles.title: Papalote mezcal, Guerrero mountain style (cupreata)
profiles.context: Guerrero is one of Mexico's great mezcal states. In its mountains the plant is called papalote — kite — for the wide, copper-toned agave the region builds its mezcal on. Families in communities like Apango roast it in earthen pits and distill small batches: the same village craft Oaxaca is famous for, in Guerrero's own voice. The name travels, though: papalote also appears in Michoacán and can name more than one cupreata-lineage agave, so the word needs its mountain context to mean anything precise.
profiles.description: Fruit comes first here, not smoke. The example bottle, from the Alcaraz family in Apango, opens with a fruit-salad nose (grape, apple, banana) and a breath of mint and green pepper, then a juicy, easy palate and a warm finish with a touch of vanilla. Heat varies from lot to lot: the same tasters find some run hot. Wild cupreata is under real pressure, and some producers answer that by planting and reforesting.
profiles.beginnerNote: New to Guerrero mezcal? Start here expecting fruit before smoke: mint, green pepper and a buttery edge over a gentle roast. Batch to batch it may pour hotter or cooler, so judge the bottle in your glass, not the region as a whole.
profiles.category: Mezcal — Guerrero lies within the mezcal denomination of origin; papalote is the regional name for a cupreata-lineage agave, not a legal class
profiles.plant: Agave cupreata (papalote; wild-harvested and cultivated)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, wild-fermented, distilled in small batches
profiles.smoke: Gentle in the cited reviews of the example bottle — the roast supports the fruit rather than leading it.
profiles.finish: Medium and warm in the example bottle's reviews, with mint and sweet vanilla notes.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass; the fruit opens with a short rest. Also works in a Margarita, where its fruit plays with citrus. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the mint-and-fruit arrival. If that welcome suits you, another Guerrero papalote is worth seeking out — expect batch variation.

profiles.whyItTastes: The cupreata here is wild and cultivated, roasted in earthen pits, fermented with wild yeasts and distilled in small batches in the mountains. In the example bottle, tasters find fruit, mint and butter sitting in front of a gentle roast. Some say mountain cupreata always puts the fruit first. It's an appealing idea, but no source shows how that would work, and one bottle doesn't speak for all of Guerrero.

profiles.title: Cenizo mezcal, Durango sierra style (Agave durangensis)
profiles.context: Durango is the north within the mezcal denomination — sierra and canyon country where a distillery is a vinata, not a palenque, and the signature agave is cenizo, named for the ash tone of its leaves. In El Mezquital, Tepehuán vinatero families like the Cruz family roast cenizo among the pines at elevation, mash by axe and desgarradora, and distill in small copper-and-wood stills. Northern is not a synonym for Oaxacan: Durango's mezcal has its own plant, vocabulary and voice.
profiles.description: Expect candy fruit: watermelon and berry sweets, bubblegum and citrus over a light roast, with a lactic, almost cheesy edge and real heat. That's the example bottle, from Federico Cruz and his Tepehuán family in El Mezquital. Most tasters call it bright, fruity and well balanced; a few have met rustic or polarising lots, and the heat varies from lot to lot. Durango producers, speaking to SevenFifty Daily, describe cenizo in general as sweet and green, fruity and earthy, with lactic notes.
profiles.beginnerNote: New to cenizo? Expect candy fruit — watermelon, berry, bubblegum — over a gentle roast, and be ready for heat: the example bottle's lots range from 49 to 54% ABV and reviewers feel it. That is the bottle and the batch, not a fixed Durango welcome.
profiles.category: Mezcal — Durango lies within the mezcal denomination of origin; cenizo is the regional name for Agave durangensis, not a legal class
profiles.plant: Agave durangensis (cenizo; mostly wild-harvested, nursery programs growing)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, mashed by axe and desgarradora, wild-fermented in pine vats, distilled in copper-and-wood stills
profiles.smoke: Light in the cited reviews of the example bottle — the pit roast is present but the fruit leads.
profiles.finish: Long and drying in several of the example bottle's reviews, with mint and mineral notes after the fruit.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass with water alongside — the cited lots run hot, and a few drops soften the heat without losing the fruit. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the candy-fruit arrival and the heat behind it. If the fruit suits you, other cenizo — from Durango or elsewhere — is worth a taste; expect each lot to read a little different.

profiles.whyItTastes: Cenizo (Agave durangensis) is mostly wild-harvested and grows mainly from seed, so each plant is genetically its own and no two batches are copies of each other. After the harvest come an underground oven, an axe and desgarradora to break up the cooked agave, wild fermentation in pine vats with spring water, and copper-and-wood stills. The producer adds that this batch's agave grew among pines at altitude, in a colder climate than most cenizo. It's tempting to credit that for the candy fruit, but the reviews don't show it, and one vinata's lots can't speak for all of Durango.

profiles.title: Maguey verde mezcal, Altiplano Potosino style (Agave salmiana)
profiles.context: On the rocky, arid Potosino plateau, the agave that endures is maguey verde — the salmiana — and hacienda families like the Hernández lineage of Santa Isabel have made mezcal from it for over a century. The same species feeds the pulque heartland farther south, but here the tradition cooks the piña mezcal-style rather than tapping sap: a different plant context and a different tradition from the destilado de pulque this guide also covers. How the plateau's agave is cooked is genuinely disputed — the producer describes a traditional clay oven, a local reviewer reports an autoclave — and the disagreement stays open on this page.
profiles.description: Green and bright, with little or no smoke: jalapeño and green pepper, cut grass, lemon and elderflower. That's how tasters describe the example bottle, made by maestro Juan José Hernández at the Santa Isabel hacienda, though they agree on little else. One calls it a soft, pretty example of the region; others find it grassy, soapy or harsh. That spread is part of the picture. Other maguey verde mezcals often pour differently.
profiles.beginnerNote: New to maguey verde? Expect a green, vegetal pour — jalapeño, grass, lemon — and very little smoke. Reviews of the example bottle are split, so taste it with food if the first sip is harsh.
profiles.category: Mezcal — San Luis Potosí lies within the mezcal denomination of origin; maguey verde is the regional salmiana name, not a legal class
profiles.plant: Agave salmiana (maguey verde; wild plateau populations, 7–10 years to maturity)
profiles.process: Cooked in the hacienda's oven tradition, wild-fermented, distilled in copper
profiles.smoke: Little to none per the cited reviews of the example bottle — reviewers who address cooking connect the low smoke to an oven rather than a pit roast.
profiles.finish: Medium in the example bottle's reviews; lemon and mineral notes.

placeCoords.precision: municipality (Santa Isabel area, San Luis Potosí); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat at room temperature in a small glass; the vegetal character also suits a salty companion (the regional serve pairs it with orange, salt and chili). Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the green, jalapeño-and-lemon character and the near-total absence of smoke — a useful contrast with pit-roasted styles.

profiles.whyItTastes: The plant is wild salmiana from the plateau, which takes seven to ten years to mature. It's cooked in the hacienda's oven, fermented with airborne wild yeasts and distilled in copper. How that oven works is disputed: the producer describes a traditional clay oven, while a local reviewer reports an autoclave. One reviewer links the oven to the green, low-smoke character, which makes sense, but while the cooking method stays unresolved the cause is an open question. What the reviews of this bottle do agree on is the green character itself.

profiles.title: Cupreata mezcal, Rio de Parras style (Michoacán)
profiles.context: Michoacán is a major mezcal state with a voice of its own: river valleys of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, Filipino-style wooden stills and fermentations that can include pulque. More than one reviewer of Michoacán mezcals describes a creamy, lactic streak in the state's cupreata and inaequidens. In the Río de Parras communities, maestra mezcalera María E. Pérez and her family call their maguey penca ancha, a local name for Agave cupreata, and their vinata starts fermentation with 10–15 litres of pulque. Penca ancha is Michoacán's name, not Guerrero's papalote: two states, two names, one wide cupreata lineage.
profiles.description: This is the creamy side of mezcal: pink bubblegum, strawberries and cream, sour fruit and grape soda, with a lactic, slightly fizzy edge. That's the example bottle, from María E. Pérez and her family in Rio de Parras. Several tasters credit the pulque that starts its fermentation, and one says those fermentation notes are what set it apart from a Guerrero cupreata. In some reviewed lots the heat stays mild for the strength, though that varies. Other Michoacán mezcals share the state's tools and habits, not one flavour.
profiles.beginnerNote: New to Michoacán mezcal? Expect the creamy side of the family: bubblegum, strawberries, and a lactic tang that is a feature of this producer's method, not a flaw. If you know Guerrero's papalote, this is the same plant lineage with a different kitchen — and a different name.
profiles.category: Mezcal — Michoacán lies within the mezcal denomination of origin; penca ancha is the regional name for Agave cupreata in Rio de Parras, not a legal class
profiles.plant: Agave cupreata (penca ancha in Rio de Parras; wild-harvested and cultivated)
profiles.process: Hand-milled with wooden mallets, pulque-started wild fermentation, Filipino-style still distillation
profiles.smoke: Light to none in the cited reviews of the example bottle — the palate leads with fruit and lactic tang, not roast smoke.
profiles.finish: Creamy and fruity in the example bottle's reviews, with a soft lactic tang; one lot shows lime rind and sea salt on the way out.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass; the creamy fruit opens with a short rest. Also works in a Margarita, where its lactic tang plays with citrus. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the bubblegum-and-cream arrival and the gentle, pulque-tinged tang behind it — this producer's signature, and a good introduction to Michoacán's style.

profiles.whyItTastes: Here the cupreata, called penca ancha, is hand-milled with wooden mallets, its fermentation is started with 10–15 litres of pulque, and it is distilled in a Filipino-style wooden still. More than one taster connects the bubblegum and lactic tang to that pulque. It's a fair, consistent reading, but no source isolates the pulque as the cause: the reviewed lots were small and also rested for months in glass. The state's region page likewise credits the wooden still with keeping Michoacán mezcal creamy and mineral, which describes the tradition rather than a measured effect. The method and the taste are both real; how one leads to the other is still an open question.

profiles.title: Papalometl mezcal, Mixteca Poblana style (Puebla)
profiles.context: Puebla is quietly one of Mexico's biggest mezcal states, and in the Mixteca Poblana hills the plant at the centre of its small-batch mezcal is the papalometl — a word that shares a Nahuatl root with Guerrero's papalote but, in this bottle's documented case, names Agave potatorum, the same species Oaxaca calls tobalá. Maestra mezcalera Fabiola Torres Monfil makes it in San Diego La Mesa Tochimilitzingo with a farmer-conservationist's hand: seed-grown agaves from her nursery, ecological restoration, and programs that let plants flower for the bats that give her brand its name. The name is the lesson: papalometl needs its state attached, because the same word can point to different agaves in different states.
profiles.description: A fruit bowl with a spark: apple pie, banana taffy, mango and pineapple, and a sharp acidity that one taster compares to vinegar or sparkling wine and another to champagne. That's the example bottle, from maestra mezcalera Fabiola Torres Monfil in San Diego La Mesa Tochimilitzingo. It varies from one small lot to the next: one fermented in rawhide comes across funkier, and some finish with plum and fig. Take it as a first taste of what Puebla's mezcal can be rather than a rule, because the same word, papalometl, can pour quite differently from another producer.
profiles.beginnerNote: New to Puebla mezcal? Expect a fruit basket with a spark: apple, banana, tropical fruit and a bright, sparkling-wine acidity. Nothing here matches the smoky welcome the word mezcal might lead you to expect — and other Puebla producers will pour differently.
profiles.category: Mezcal — Puebla lies within the mezcal denomination of origin; papalometl is a regional plant name (potatorum in this bottle's documented case), not a legal class
profiles.plant: Agave potatorum (papalometl in the Mixteca Poblana; wild and seed-grown from the producer's nursery)
profiles.process: Pit roast, mechanical shredder, dry-then-wet wild fermentation (up to 14+5-10 days; some batches in rawhide), single distillation in copper or clay
profiles.smoke: Light in the cited reviews of the example bottle — the pit roast is present but the fruit and acidity lead.
profiles.finish: Fruity and floral in the example bottle's reviews, with a bright acidic snap; some lots finish mineral over dark fruits like plum and fig.

placeCoords.precision: municipality (San Diego La Mesa Tochimilitzingo, Puebla); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass; the acidity makes it a lively food mezcal. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.
pairing.notice: What to notice first: the apple-and-tropical-fruit arrival and the bright, almost sparkling-wine acidity behind it — the signature of this producer's papalometl, and a lively first taste of Puebla's mezcal.

profiles.whyItTastes: The papalometl here is potatorum, some wild and some grown from seed in the producer's own nursery. It's roasted in an earthen pit and shredded by machine, then fermented wild: dry for up to 14 days, then with water for another 5–10, with some small batches in rawhide. It's distilled once, in copper or clay. You might guess that the dry-then-wet fermentation sharpens the acidity, but the reviews don't say so: they report the acidity, not its cause, and a producer visit describes the house's mezcals as clean rather than funky. So the link stays open.
